…are indeed mostly men of talent, yet there are those who spurn and belittle moral conduct and reputation, stepping outside the bounds of restraint; the frontiers are peaceful, and marching gags need no longer be used, yet the soldiers are unruly and arrogant, at times giving rein to the rebellion of gathering in mutinous clamor; the supervision and capture of bandits are strict, and the night-watchman's clappers and bells could gradually be withdrawn, yet brigands in the marshes appear and disappear, at times indulging in the harm of plunder and pillage. What Your Sacred Inquiry expresses concern over, even your servant privately wonders about.

Yet in your servant's humble view, what the sage cannot guarantee is the complete order of the realm, whereas what he can exhaust his efforts in is the cultivation of the three virtues. If virtue is truly cultivated, even if the effects of good governance have not yet been fully achieved, it is not enough to be cause for alarm; if virtue is not truly cultivated, even if the effects of governance are worthy of recounting, it is still enough to be cause for worry. Therefore, Yao, Shun, and the Three Kings did not inquire about the floodwaters over which they sighed, but inquired whether the vision of the four quarters and the hearing of the four quarters had not yet been reached; they did not fear the artful and insinuating flatterers, but feared that knowing men and giving peace to the people had not yet been exhausted; they did not worry about the officers of Shang, but worried that they had not yet been able to augustly revere their own virtue; they were not anxious over the recalcitrant subjects, but were anxious that their dwelling in "Without Idleness" had not yet been carried to the utmost.

Now Your Majesty's benevolence is already vast, your perspicacity is already comprehensive, and in facing critical moments your decisiveness has already been shown. Yet what your foolish servant earnestly desires is solely to wish that Your Majesty not regard this as already sufficient, but strive ever more diligently to cultivate them. For benevolence does not mean merely prizing virtue and relaxing punishments in a petty, indulgent manner; perspicacity does not mean merely exposing villainy and ferreting out hidden crimes in a琐碎, vexatious, and harsh manner; and martial vigor does not mean merely letting severity prevail over love in a fierce, overbearing, and violent manner. Their substance must be complete, and their application must hit the mean—it is simply like this and nothing more. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would further cultivate their completeness so as to broaden the foundation of governance for the realm: let benevolence be sufficient to nurture, yet…

title: 萬曆十一年進士登科錄
text:
不專尚仁明足以照而不專尚明武足以斷
而不專尚武如天之雨露日月雷霆同運竝
行而推之課吏阜民作人治軍弭盜之際皆
是三德之誕布焉使天下曉然見全德而曰
大聖人之備道立極如斯也又益修其中者以為
天下運治機仁無不冒而不流於靡明無不
燭而不傷於煩武無不斷而不至於猛如天
之雨露日月雷霆適時中節而達之課吏阜
民作人治軍弭盜之際皆是三德之順施焉
使天下曉然見中德而曰
===
大聖人之大中至正如此也由是張弛操縱何往
而不宜拱挹指撝何施而不可𠥼飭吏治則
皐夔為之使何憂乎滋玩以厚民生則卓魯
為之牧何憂乎滋困以端士習則蘇湖為之
倡何憂乎滋偷以訓軍旅則頗牧為之用何
憂乎滋譁以弭寇盜則龔遂虞詡為之宣力
而立功又何憂乎滋起也哉此臣所以願
陛下之益懋修其德也抑臣又有
獻焉帝王之治本於道道本於德而德又本於
心心也者仁明武之所自出也臣願

punctuated:
不專尚仁，明足以照而不專尚明，武足以斷而不專尚武。如天之雨露、日月、雷霆同運竝行，而推之課吏、阜民、作人、治軍、弭盜之際，皆是三德之誕布焉，使天下曉然見全德而曰：「大聖人之備道立極如斯也！」又益修其中者，以為天下運治機。仁無不冒而不流於靡，明無不燭而不傷於煩，武無不斷而不至於猛。如天之雨露、日月、雷霆適時中節，而達之課吏、阜民、作人、治軍、弭盜之際，皆是三德之順施焉，使天下曉然見中德而曰：「大聖人之大中至正如此也！」由是張弛操縱，何往而不宜？拱挹指撝，何施而不可？𠥼飭吏治，則皐、夔為之使，何憂乎滋玩？以厚民生，則卓、魯為之牧，何憂乎滋困？以端士習，則蘇湖為之倡，何憂乎滋偷？以訓軍旅，則頗、牧為之用，何憂乎滋譁？以弭寇盜，則龔遂、虞詡為之宣力而立功，又何憂乎滋起也哉？此臣所以願陛下之益懋修其德也。

抑臣又有獻焉。帝王之治本於道，道本於德，而德又本於心。心也者，仁、明、武之所自出也。臣願
translation_en:
…not exclusively exalt benevolence; that your perspicacity be sufficient to illuminate, yet not exclusively exalt perspicacity; and that your martial vigor be sufficient to decide, yet not exclusively exalt martial vigor. Just as Heaven’s rain and dew, sun and moon, and thunderbolts operate together and proceed in parallel, when extended to the tasks of evaluating officials, enriching the people, cultivating men of talent, governing the military, and quelling bandits, all will be the grand manifestation of these three virtues, causing the whole world to clearly behold your complete virtue and declare: "Such is the way the Great Sage perfects the Way and establishes the Supreme Standard!" Furthermore, may you increasingly cultivate their due measure, thereby setting in motion the mechanisms of governance for the Empire. Your benevolence will shelter all without lapsing into weakness; your perspicacity will illuminate all without degenerating into pettiness; your martial vigor will decide all without reaching the point of ferocity. Just as Heaven’s rain and dew, sun and moon, and thunderbolts match the seasons and hit the proper measure, when applied to the tasks of evaluating officials, enriching the people, cultivating men of talent, governing the military, and quelling bandits, all will be the harmonious application of these three virtues, causing the whole world to clearly behold your balanced virtue and declare: "Such is the supreme balance and utmost rectitude of the Great Sage!" From this, in tightening or relaxing, grasping or releasing, where could you go that would not be fitting? In folding your hands or gesturing in command, what measure could you enact that would not succeed? In rectifying the administration of officials, men like Gao Yao 皐陶 and Kui 夔 will serve as your envoys—what worry could there be of growing negligence? In training the military forces, generals like Lian Po 廉頗 and Li Mu 李牧 will be in your employ—what worry could there be of growing mutiny? The mind-and-heart is that from which benevolence, perspicacity, and martial vigor issue forth. Your servant wishes that…

title: 萬曆十一年進士登科錄
text:
陛下豫養於淵微邃密之中而豫防於視聽言動
之頃講學窮理以明此心考古鏡今以惕此
心親近正人君子以夾輔此心日聞正議讜
言以弼直此心一玩好則曰心得無溺乎一
美麗則曰心得無蕩乎一馳騁則曰心得無
荒乎一貨賄則曰心得無雜乎一興作則曰
心得無侈乎諸凡有累於心者悉以為有妨
於德而斥遠之屏絕之必日兢如堯日業如
舜惡旨酒如禹不邇不殖如湯不盤遊田如
文不役耳目如武則一心之中與於穆同體
===
而三德之真宰已立矣由是一念之慈祥即
謂之仁天下所以藹然而懷也一念之靈瑩
即謂之明天下所以洞然而見也一念之震
竦即謂之武天下所以凛然而懾也蓋其效

translation_en: … that Your Majesty cultivate it beforehand in the deep, subtle, and secluded recesses of your being, and guard it beforehand at every moment of seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting. Discuss learning and exhaustively investigate principle in order to illuminate this mind; examine antiquity and mirror the present in order to keep this mind vigilant; draw close to upright men and noble persons in order to support and assist this mind; and daily hear upright discussions and forthright counsel in order to correct and straighten this mind. Faced with a curiosity or pastime, say: "Could my mind be indulging in this?" Faced with beauty and finery, say: "Could my mind be led astray by this?" Faced with galloping and hunting, say: "Could my mind be growing neglectful through this?" Faced with wealth and goods, say: "Could my mind be losing its purity over this?" Faced with a construction project, say: "Could my mind be turning extravagant in this?" Everything that might encumber the mind should be regarded as harmful to virtue, and thus rejected, kept at a distance, and banished altogether. If you are daily cautious like Yao, daily diligent like Shun, averse to fine wine like Yu, neither approaching sensual pleasures nor hoarding wealth like Tang, not indulging in pleasure excursions or hunting like King Wen, and not enslaving the ears and eyes to desires like King Wu, then within this single mind you will share the same substance as the august and profound Heaven, and the true master of the three virtues will already be established. From this, a single thought of kindness and benevolence is itself humanity (ren), whereby the world is harmoniously drawn to cherish you; a single thought of spiritual clarity is itself discernment (ming), whereby the world is thoroughly seen and understood; and a single thought of awe-inspiring resolution is itself martial vigor (wu), whereby the world stands in reverent dread. Indeed, its effect is most vast, its response most swift, and its pivotal mechanism lies solely in Your Majesty's single mind. May Your Sacred Brilliance pay heed to this. Your servant is a scholar from the rustic wilds, ignorant of taboos; having offended the Imperial Majesty, I am overcome with trembling and the fear of falling into ruin. Your servant respectfully replies.

title: 萬曆十一年進士登科錄
text:
臣劉應秋
臣對臣聞帝王之治天下也必出之以全德
而後可以裕經制之宏規必本之以實心而
後可以達時宜之妙用何者天下至大也民
物至庶也萬幾之務至殷且繁也君人者以
一人而撫有天下握民物之紀總幾務之繁
舉天下環嚮而待澤者何限匪恩惠固無以
紓天下之困而恩勝則易敧或者優柔而弗
振舉天下拱揖而聽命者何限匪明斷固無
以釐天下之姦而過察則寡恩恐以猛厲而
===
召釁然使矯飾乎兼體之彌文而行之不實
襲取乎一時之虛聲而本之則無則寬嚴弛
張之權既以乖盭而無序政治教化之行必
且壅閼而弗達持此以理吾未見其可矣是
故智仁勇三者德之全也所以為宰制天下
之紀綱不可使其或闕也而誠也者尤三德
之原也所以為運量天下之精神不可使其
有偽也有是宰制天下之全德故紀綱丕振
於朝堂而德化旁敷于海寓剛克柔克必無
偏詖而不舉有是運量天下之實心故精神

臣劉應秋。
臣對：臣聞帝王之治天下也，必出之以全德，而後可以裕經制之宏規；必本之以實心，而後可以達時宜之妙用。何者？天下至大也，民物至庶也，萬幾之務至殷且繁也。君人者，以一人而撫有天下，握民物之紀，總幾務之繁。舉天下環嚮而待澤者何限，匪恩惠固無以紓天下之困，而恩勝則易敧，或者優柔而弗振；舉天下拱揖而聽命者何限，匪明斷固無以釐天下之姦，而過察則寡恩，恐以猛厲而召釁。然使矯飾乎兼體之彌文，而行之不實；襲取乎一時之虛聲，而本之則無，則寬嚴弛張之權，既以乖盭而無序；政治教化之行，必且壅閼而弗達。持此以理，吾未見其可矣。是故智、仁、勇三者，德之全也，所以為宰制天下之紀綱，不可使其或闕也；而誠也者，尤三德之原也，所以為運量天下之精神，不可使其有偽也。有是宰制天下之全德，故紀綱丕振於朝堂，而德化旁敷于海寓，剛克柔克，必無偏詖而不舉；有是運量天下之實心，故精神
translation_en:
Your servant Liu Yingqiu 劉應秋.
Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that when emperors and kings govern All under Heaven, their governance must issue from complete virtue before they can enrich the grand framework of state institutions, and it must be rooted in a sincere mind before they can achieve the wondrous efficacy of measures suited to the times. Why is this? All under Heaven is vast, the people and myriad things are numerous, and the myriad affairs of state are most pressing and complex. One who rules over men possesses All under Heaven as a single person, holding the guiding threads of the people and things and overseeing the complexity of state affairs. Across the entire empire, how limitless are those who turn toward him in anticipation of his beneficence! Without grace and kindness, there is truly no way to relieve the distress of the empire; yet if grace prevails excessively, it easily tilts into imbalance, perhaps becoming indulgent, weak, and unenergetic. Across the entire empire, how limitless are those who bow with folded hands to await his commands! Without clear-sighted decisiveness, there is truly no way to root out the villainy of the empire; yet if scrutiny is excessive, kindness becomes scarce, and one fears provoking strife through fierce severity. However, if one merely contrives the superficial trappings of combining both approaches while failing to practice them with sincerity, or appropriates empty renown for the moment while lacking a genuine foundation, then the balance of leniency and strictness, of relaxation and tension, will become perverse and disorderly, and the implementation of governance and moral transformation will inevitably become obstructed and fail to reach everywhere. To hold to such a course in governing—I cannot see how it could succeed. Therefore, wisdom, benevolence, and courage are the completeness of virtue; they serve as the fundamental order by which All under Heaven is directed and regulated, and none of them may be lacking. And sincerity is above all the source of these three virtues; it serves as the vital spirit by which All under Heaven is moved and measured, and it must not be allowed any falsehood. Possessing this complete virtue for directing and regulating All under Heaven, the fundamental order is greatly invigorated in the court, and moral transformation spreads widely throughout the realm; whether overcoming by firmness or overcoming by gentleness, there will surely be nothing one-sided or neglected. Possessing this sincere mind for moving and measuring All under Heaven, the vital spirit…

title: 萬曆十一年進士登科錄
text:
默運於沕穆而意指大順于域中用威用愛
亦何所施而不當自昔帝王恩足以洽羣生
而其惠不費知足以鏡萬物而其明不苛斷
足以裁庶務而其政不猛惠不費天下稱至
仁焉明不苛天下稱大智焉政不猛天下稱
神勇焉其治成蕩巍而化登熈皞也何莫不
繇斯道哉欽惟
皇帝陛下
躬不世出之資
具大有為之畧
===
孝養純至弘錫類于八紘
問學精勤樹風教於九有邇益
明習政體
親决幾疑
離照無私燭極日月之表
乾剛獨斷赫若雷霆之威
長育與震曜竝行
惇大兼明作交懋雕題鑿齒之域重譯貢珍日
氏月窟之邦稽首納欵五辰順軌四海安瀾
九扈告豐諸福荐至斯熈洽之盛際泰寧之

默運於沕穆，而意指大順于域中，用威用愛，亦何所施而不當？自昔帝王，恩足以洽羣生，而其惠不費；知足以鏡萬物，而其明不苛；斷足以裁庶務，而其政不猛。惠不費，天下稱至仁焉；明不苛，天下稱大智焉；政不猛，天下稱神勇焉。其治成蕩巍，而化登熈皞也，何莫不繇斯道哉！
欽惟皇帝陛下，躬不世出之資，具大有為之畧。孝養純至，弘錫類于八紘；問學精勤，樹風教於九有。邇益明習政體，親决幾疑。離照無私，燭極日月之表；乾剛獨斷，赫若雷霆之威。長育與震曜竝行，惇大兼明作交懋。雕題鑿齒之域，重譯貢珍；日氏月窟之邦，稽首納欵。五辰順軌，四海安瀾，九扈告豐，諸福荐至。斯熈洽之盛際，泰寧之
translation_en:
… operates silently in profound subtlety, and the imperial will meets with great compliance throughout the realm; whether employing awe or employing affection, wherever it is applied, how could it ever fail to be fitting? From of old, with the emperors and kings, their grace was sufficient to steep all living beings, yet their beneficence was not wasteful; their wisdom was sufficient to mirror the myriad things, yet their discernment was not harsh; their decisiveness was sufficient to adjudicate the multitude of affairs, yet their governance was not fierce. Because their beneficence was not wasteful, all under Heaven acclaimed them as supremely benevolent; because their discernment was not harsh, all under Heaven acclaimed them as greatly wise; because their governance was not fierce, all under Heaven acclaimed them as divinely courageous. That their governance achieved vast and lofty perfection, and their transformative influence ascended to harmonious and radiant peace—how could any of this not have proceeded from this Way!

Your servant reverently reflects that Your Majesty the Emperor embodies talents that appear but once in an epoch, and possesses the grand strategy for great achievements. Your filial nourishment is pure and utmost, broadly extending unfailing kindness to the eight extremities of the world; your inquiry and learning are refined and diligent, establishing moral instruction across the nine regions. Of late, you have grown ever more versed in the substance of governance, personally deciding subtle and doubtful matters. Your Li-trigram illumination is impartial, shining to the farthest reaches beyond the sun and moon; your Qian-trigram firmness decides alone, awesome as the might of thunder and lightning. Nurturing growth and awesome splendor proceed side by side; generous magnanimity and clear, energetic action are mutually encouraged in tandem. The regions of tattooed foreheads and chiseled teeth present precious tribute through repeated translations; the lands where the sun rests [?] and the moon has its cavern bow their heads to the ground and offer allegiance. The five seasonalcelestial motions follow their proper courses, the Four Seas calm their waves, the nine agricultural bird-officials announce abundant harvests, and all blessings arrive in succession. This is indeed a flourishing era of harmonious concord, and the … of great peace and tranquility.

title: 萬曆十一年進士登科錄
text:
休風也已乃猶
聖不自聖進臣等于
廷
俯賜
清問豈以藜藿之中亦有達治理識世務其人乎
臣愚沐浴
聖化願攄忠悃之日久矣嘗謂人主有求言之令
則必有納言之實人臣遇得言之日不可無
獻言之誠臣今幸際
聖明獲奉
===
休命得言其時矣敢不披瀝以對臣聞之書曰天
佑下民作之君作之師惟其克相上帝寵綏
四方盖天有安民之心而不能以自遂也故
以治教之責寄之乎君君有代天之任而非
可以自私也故以治教之道法之乎天天以
雨露潤萬物人君法之以育天下其道曰仁
天以日月照萬物人君法之以察天下其道
曰智天以霜雪剥萬物人君法之以裁天下
其道曰勇是故孔子告魯君為政以此三達
德為九經之要而司馬光歷陳宋主亦必曰

休風也已。乃猶聖不自聖，進臣等于廷，俯賜清問，豈以藜藿之中，亦有達治理、識世務其人乎？臣愚沐浴聖化，願攄忠悃之日久矣。嘗謂人主有求言之令，則必有納言之實；人臣遇得言之日，不可無獻言之誠。臣今幸際聖明，獲奉休命，得言其時矣，敢不披瀝以對？

臣聞之《書》曰：「天佑下民，作之君，作之師，惟其克相上帝，寵綏四方。」盖天有安民之心，而不能以自遂也，故以治教之責寄之乎君；君有代天之任，而非可以自私也，故以治教之道法之乎天。天以雨露潤萬物，人君法之以育天下，其道曰仁；天以日月照萬物，人君法之以察天下，其道曰智；天以霜雪剥萬物，人君法之以裁天下，其道曰勇。是故孔子告魯君為政，以此三達德為九經之要；而司馬光歷陳宋主，亦必曰
translation_en:
…auspicious customs indeed! Yet Your Majesty still does not regard Yourself as a sage, advancing Your servants to the court and graciously bestowing Your clear inquiry. Could it be because You consider that even among those who live on coarse greens there are men who comprehend the principles of governance and understand the affairs of the world? In my simplicity, I, Your servant, have long been bathed in Your sacred transformation and wished for the day to pour forth my loyal sincerity. I have always held that when a ruler issues an order seeking counsel, there must be the reality of accepting counsel; and when a subject encounters a day on which he is permitted to speak, he cannot lack the sincerity to offer counsel. Today, Your servant is fortunate to encounter Your Sacred Brilliance and to receive Your gracious command; the time to speak has arrived—how could I dare not lay bare my heart in reply?

Your servant has heard that the Book of Documents (Shu) says: "Heaven protects the people below, and made for them rulers, and made for them instructors, simply that they might be able to assist God On High and lovingly secure the four quarters of the empire." Indeed, Heaven has the heart to bring peace to the people, yet cannot accomplish this by itself; therefore, it entrusts the responsibility of governing and instructing to the ruler. The ruler bears the duty of acting on behalf of Heaven, and cannot treat it as his private possession; therefore, he models his Way of governing and instructing upon Heaven. Heaven moistens the myriad things with rain and dew, and the ruler models himself on this to nurture the empire: its Way is called benevolence. Heaven illuminates the myriad things with the sun and moon, and the ruler models himself on this to scrutinize the empire: its Way is called wisdom. Heaven strips the myriad things with frost and snow, and the ruler models himself on this to regulate the empire: its Way is called courage. title: 萬曆十一年進士登科錄
text:
仁明武其說盖本諸孔子詳哉乎其言之矣
夫所謂仁者非姑息之謂也以寬厚御羣下
以德澤撫黎庶如是而已一於仁必且優游
而無斷所謂智者非任術之謂也明邪正之
幾辨忠佞之實如是而已一於智必且苛察
而多疑所謂勇者非尚刑之謂也操大權以
折姦萌布聖武以遏亂畧如是而已一於勇
必且亢暴而輕僨是知此三德者闕一不可
也闕一則衰闕二則危非虛語也道固然也
粤稽古史盖有明徵焉稱堯曰其仁如天其
===
知如神稱舜曰明物察倫由仁義行稱禹曰
其仁可親其言可信似若未及武矣然而四
兇之誅三苗之征亦何甞盡廢武哉言仁明
而武可知也在成湯則有天錫勇智之稱在
武王則有執競維烈之頌似若始尚武矣然
而子惠困窮愛育黎首亦何甞專用武哉言
武而仁明可知也盖堯舜禹以文德綏太平
湯武以武功戡禍亂故所稱各殊二帝兼而
帝三代兼而王而誠心則同嗣是以降乃有
少謬不然者論開創則漢稱高光唐稱太宗
alt_text:
仁明武其說盖本諸孔子詳哉乎其言之矣
夫所謂仁者非姑息之謂也以寛厚御羣下
以德澤撫黎庶如是而已一於仁必且優游
而無斷所謂智者非任術之謂也明邪正之
幾辨忠佞之實如是而已一於智必且苛察
而多疑所謂勇者非尚刑之謂也操大權以
折姦萌布聖武以遏亂畧如是而已一於勇
必且亢暴而輕僨是知此三德者闕一不可
也闕一則衰闕二則危非虛語也道固然也
粤稽古史盖有明徵焉稱堯曰其仁如天其
===
知如神稱舜曰明明物察倫由仁義行稱禹曰
其仁可親其言可信似若未及武矣然而四
凶之誅三苗之征亦何嘗盡廢武哉言仁明
而武可知也在成湯則有天錫勇智之稱在
武王則有執競維烈之頌似若始尚武矣然
而子惠困窮愛育黎首亦何嘗專用武哉言
武而仁明可知也盖堯舜禹以文德綏太平
湯武以武功戡禍亂故所稱各殊二帝兼而
帝三代兼而王而誠心則同嗣是以降乃有
少謬不然者論開創則漢稱高光唐稱太宗
punctuated:
仁、明、武。其說盖本諸孔子，詳哉乎其言之矣！夫所謂仁者，非姑息之謂也，以寬厚御羣下，以德澤撫黎庶，如是而已。一於仁，必且優游而無斷。所謂智者，非任術之謂也，明邪正之幾，辨忠佞之實，如是而已。一於智，必且苛察而多疑。所謂勇者，非尚刑之謂也，操大權以折姦萌，布聖武以遏亂畧，如是而已。一於勇，必且亢暴而輕僨。是知此三德者，闕一不可也。闕一則衰，闕二則危，非虛語也，道固然也。
粤稽古史，盖有明徵焉。稱堯曰「其仁如天，其知如神」；稱舜曰「明物察倫，由仁義行」；稱禹曰「其仁可親，其言可信」，似若未及武矣。然而四兇之誅、三苗之征，亦何甞盡廢武哉？言仁明而武可知也。在成湯則有「天錫勇智」之稱，在武王則有「執競維烈」之頌，似若始尚武矣。然而「子惠困窮」、「愛育黎首」，亦何甞專用武哉？言武而仁明可知也。盖堯、舜、禹以文德綏太平，湯、武以武功戡禍亂，故所稱各殊。二帝兼而帝，三代兼而王，而誠心則同。嗣是以降，乃有少謬不然者。論開創，則漢稱高、光，唐稱太宗，
translation_en:
… benevolence, discernment, and martial vigor. His argument was in fact grounded in Confucius—how thorough indeed were his words! Now, what is called benevolence does not mean indulgent leniency; it is simply governing the multitude of subordinates with magnanimity and thickness of grace, and comforting the common people with virtuous beneficence—nothing more than this. If one relies exclusively on benevolence, one will inevitably become indecisive and lacking in resolution. What is called wisdom does not mean employing manipulative statecraft; it is simply discerning the subtle signs of crookedness and rectitude, and distinguishing the reality of loyalty and flattery—nothing more than this. If one relies exclusively on wisdom, one will inevitably become overly fastidious in scrutiny and full of suspicion. What is called courage does not mean prizing punishments; it is simply wielding great authority to nip treacherous plots in the bud, and displaying sacred martial vigor to stem rebellious designs—nothing more than this. If one relies exclusively on courage, one will inevitably become overbearing, violent, and rashly ruinous. From this we know that of these three virtues, not a single one can be lacking. That lacking one leads to decline and lacking two leads to peril is no empty saying; the Way is inherently so.

If we examine ancient history, there is clear evidence of this. Yao 堯 is praised with the words, "His benevolence was like Heaven, his wisdom like a spirit"; Shun 舜 is praised with the words, "He clearly understood things and examined human relationships, acting out of benevolence and righteousness"; Yu 禹 is praised with the words, "His benevolence was approachable, his words trustworthy." It would seem as though martial vigor was not mentioned for them. Yet in the punishment of the Four Criminals (Sixiong 四兇) and the punitive expedition against the Three Miao (Sanmiao 三苗), how did they ever completely abandon martial vigor? When benevolence and discernment are spoken of, their martial vigor can be known by implication. In the case of Tang the Accomplished (Cheng Tang 成湯), there was the praise that "Heaven endowed him with courage and wisdom"; in the case of King Wu (Wuwang 武王), there was the eulogy that "he held fast to strength, and majestic was his achievement." It would seem as though martial vigor first came to be prized with them. Yet in "cherishing the distressed and impoverished like children" and "lovingly nurturing the black-haired people," how did they ever rely exclusively on martial vigor? When martial vigor is spoken of, their benevolence and discernment can be known by implication. Indeed, Yao, Shun, and Yu pacified an era of great peace through civil virtue, whereas Tang and King Wu quelled disasters and rebellions through martial merit; therefore, what was praised in each differed. The Two Emperors combined these virtues to rule as emperors, and the founders of the Three Dynasties combined them to rule as kings, while their sincere minds were the same. From that time onward, however, there were those who erred slightly and fell short of this. Speaking of dynastic founders, the Han 漢 acclaims Emperors Gaozu (Gao 高) and Guangwu (Guang 光), the Tang 唐 acclaims Emperor Taizong 太宗, …

title: 萬曆十一年進士登科錄
text:
宋稱藝祖皆為偉畧隆基之主然三德未純
僅可以肇造洪緒而不可以登閎治古是亦
不純之弊章章明也論繼體則漢有孝文孝
武唐有明皇武皇宋有仁宗英宗並稱守成
纘業之君然一德偏具亦可以增光宗祏而
不可以致治棊隆則其偏具之弊昭昭著也
當時諸臣誥誡非無補偏救弊之說匡衡以
六戒疏曰戒大察曰戒無斷陸贄以九弊陳
曰眩聰明曰勵威強蘇軾以六事上曰不喜
兵刑曰不用智數使世主能采而行之雖未
===
必即可以追三德之治亦或可以挽末流之
趨而柰之何寬柔因任者甘心于藏疾之汙
刑名煩苛者自貽其剛愎之禍盖心非幾于
粹白道未協於純固此其治效之卑卑而日
尋於覆轍也又何惑哉
皇上臨御以來德澤覃敷泰道一新蠲租寬刑春
膏普而涸鱗再起剗姦剔邪太陽出而魑魅
潛消十有一年之間化成弦歌俗歸長厚九
邊淨狼煙之警四郊無萑苻之憂天下稱已
治已安矣而

punctuated:
宋稱藝祖，皆為偉畧隆基之主。然三德未純，僅可以肇造洪緒，而不可以登閎治古，是亦不純之弊章章明也。論繼體，則漢有孝文、孝武，唐有明皇、武皇，宋有仁宗、英宗，並稱守成纘業之君。然一德偏具，亦可以增光宗祏，而不可以致治棊隆，則其偏具之弊昭昭著也。當時諸臣誥誡，非無補偏救弊之說：匡衡以六戒疏，曰「戒大察」，曰「戒無斷」；陸贄以九弊陳，曰「眩聰明」，曰「勵威強」；蘇軾以六事上，曰「不喜兵刑」，曰「不用智數」。使世主能采而行之，雖未必即可以追三德之治，亦或可以挽末流之趨。而柰之何寬柔因任者，甘心于藏疾之汙；刑名煩苛者，自貽其剛愎之禍？盖心非幾于粹白，道未協於純固，此其治效之卑卑，而日尋於覆轍也，又何惑哉！
皇上臨御以來，德澤覃敷，泰道一新。蠲租寬刑，春膏普而涸鱗再起；剗姦剔邪，太陽出而魑魅潛消。十有一年之間，化成弦歌，俗歸長厚，九邊淨狼煙之警，四郊無萑苻之憂，天下稱已治已安矣。而
translation_en:
…and the Song praises its Accomplished Progenitor (Emperor Taizu)—all were rulers of grand strategy who laid great foundations. Yet because the three virtues in them were not pure, they could only initiate their grand enterprises, and could not ascend to the expansive governance of antiquity; thus the flaw of their lack of purity is abundantly clear. When we discuss succeeding rulers, the Han had Filial Wen and Filial Wu, the Tang had the Illustrious August Emperor (Xuanzong) and the Martial August Emperor (Wuzong), and the Song had Renzong and Yingzong, all of whom were alike praised as sovereigns who preserved the achievements and continued the enterprises of their predecessors. Yet because they possessed only a single virtue in a one-sided manner, while they could add luster to their ancestral temples, they could not bring about the supreme flourishing of governance; thus the flaw of their one-sided possession is manifestly evident. The admonitions of the various ministers of those times were not without doctrines for remedying partiality and rescuing from abuses: Kuang Heng匡衡 submitted a memorial on Six Admonitions, saying "guard against excessive scrutiny" and "guard against indecisiveness"; Lu Zhi 陸贄 set forth Nine Abuses, speaking of "dazzling others with one's intelligence" and "striving to display awe and might"; Su Shi 蘇軾 presented Six Matters, speaking of "not delighting in military force and punishments" and "not employing cleverness and calculation." Had the rulers of those ages been able to adopt and practice these counsels, even if they might not immediately have matched the governance of the three virtues, they might perhaps have turned back the tendencies of a declining age. Yet how was it that those who were lenient, pliant, and passively reliant willingly rested in the filth of harboring maladies, while those devoted to legalist accountability and vexatious harshness brought upon themselves the disasters of obstinacy and self-will? It is because their minds did not approach pure whiteness, and their Way did not harmonize with unadulterated firmness. That the results of their governance were so paltry, and that day after day they followed in the tracks of overturned carts—what wonder is it!

Since Your Majesty ascended the throne, Your virtuous beneficence has spread far and wide, and the Way of great peace has been wholly renewed. Remitting taxes and relaxing punishments, the spring rains fall universally and fish in dried-up ruts revive once more; cutting down the treacherous and rooting out the perverse, the great sun comes forth and mountain sprites and evil spirits secretly vanish. Within the space of eleven years, teaching has been transformed into the music of stringed instruments and song, and customs have returned to generosity and thickness; the Nine Frontiers are cleansed of the alarms of wolf-dung beacons, and the four outskirts are free from the worries of bandits in the reed marshes. All under heaven acclaims the realm as already well-governed and already secure! And yet…

title: 萬曆十一年進士登科錄
text:
聖心方且兢兢夕惕晨興不遑寧處伏讀
聖制有曰紀綱飭而吏滋玩田野墾而民滋困學
校肅而士滋偷邊鄙寧而兵滋譁督捕嚴而盜
滋起厥咎安在豈朕仁未溥與明或蔽與當幾
而少斷與大哉
皇言若歆然於三德之用有未盡當者臣有以知
陛下此心即堯舜兢業之心也即禹湯文武憂勤
之心也顧今日天下之患豈惟
陛下疑之即臣亦竊疑之矣禁貪除暴之令日申
而肥瘠秦越脂韋如飴者接踵也清丈闢墾
===
之法雖行而室如懸磬野有啼饑者枕籍也
學政非不申飭而士習未盡歸淳盜禁非不
嚴緝而草澤間或竊發頃者緬甸繹騷而邊
境且告擾矣山陝流徙而姦民且生變矣誠
有以廑
宵旰之慮也臣愚計之其何策而可夫吏治之滋
玩者文法勝也今之責成長吏不過簿書期
會之間而催科後期則有罰積穀不足則有
罰彼為長吏方汲汲取盈以救過之不暇烏
覩所謂民瘼哉誠寬之文法而無以繭絲先

punctuated: 聖心方且兢兢，夕惕晨興，不遑寧處。伏讀聖制有曰：「紀綱飭而吏滋玩，田野墾而民滋困，學校肅而士滋偷，邊鄙寧而兵滋譁，督捕嚴而盜滋起。厥咎安在？豈朕仁未溥與？明或蔽與？當幾而少斷與？」大哉皇言！若歆然於三德之用有未盡當者。臣有以知陛下此心，即堯、舜兢業之心也，即禹、湯、文、武憂勤之心也。顧今日天下之患，豈惟陛下疑之，即臣亦竊疑之矣。禁貪除暴之令日申，而肥瘠秦、越，脂韋如飴者接踵也；清丈闢墾之法雖行，而室如懸磬，野有啼饑者枕籍也；學政非不申飭，而士習未盡歸淳；盜禁非不嚴緝，而草澤間或竊發。頃者緬甸繹騷，而邊境且告擾矣；山、陝流徙，而姦民且生變矣。誠有以廑宵旰之慮也。臣愚計之，其何策而可？夫吏治之滋玩者，文法勝也。今之責成長吏，不過簿書期會之間，而催科後期則有罰，積穀不足則有罰。彼為長吏，方汲汲取盈以救過之不暇，烏覩所謂民瘼哉？誠寬之文法，而無以繭絲先
translation_en:
… Your Sacred Mind remains ever cautious and apprehensive, vigilant by night and rising at dawn, having no leisure to rest in peace. Humbly reading Your Sacred Decree, I find the words: "State discipline is tightened, yet officials grow ever more lax; fields and wilds are opened to cultivation, yet the people grow ever more distressed; schools are made solemn, yet scholars grow ever more frivolous; the frontiers are peaceful, yet the soldiers grow ever more mutinous; the supervision of arrests is strict, yet bandits arise in ever greater numbers. Wherein lies the fault? Could it be that Our benevolence is not yet widespread? That Our discernment is somehow obscured? Or that at critical moments We lack decisiveness?" Great indeed are the Imperial words! It is as though You feel modestly dissatisfied that Your application of the Three Virtues has not been entirely fitting. Your servant knows by this that Your Majesty's mind is none other than the cautious and industrious mind of Yao and Shun, and none other than the anxious and diligent mind of Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu.

Yet as for the afflictions of the empire today, how could it be only Your Majesty who is perplexed by them? Even Your servant privately feels perplexed by them as well. Orders prohibiting corruption and eradicating cruelty are reiterated daily, yet those who regard the people's weal and woe with the indifference of Qin toward Yue, and who fawn and flatter as if it were sweet syrup, follow one upon another's heels; laws for surveying land and opening new fields are carried out, yet homes are as empty as hangingstone chimes, and in the countryside those crying out in hunger lie strewn upon one another; school administration is by no means left unrectified, yet the habits of scholars have not wholly returned to honest simplicity; prohibitions against banditry are by no means loosely enforced, yet in the wilds and marshes outbreaks still secretly occur from time to time. Recently, Burma (Miandian) has been in turmoil, and the frontier regions have reported disturbances; in Shanxi and Shaanxi people have been displaced and wandering, and wicked subjects have even stirred up revolt. Truly, there is cause to burden Your anxious thoughts before dawn and after dusk.

In Your servant's humble estimation, by what policy can this be remedied? Now, the reason official administration grows ever more lax is that legalistic formalities prevail. Today, what is demanded of chief local officials amounts to nothing more than registers, documents, and scheduled deadlines: if tax collection falls behind schedule, there is a penalty; if stored grain is insufficient, there is a penalty. Those who serve as chief officials are so busily preoccupied with meeting full quotas so as to save themselves from blame that they have no time to spare—how then could they pay heed to the so-called sufferings of the people? If only legalistic formalities were relaxed for them, and exacting revenues like unwinding silk from a cocoon were not put ahead of…
